discoveryHook.scenario: When we compare two sample variances, their ratio follows a special curve called the F‑distribution. It helps us decide if one variance is really bigger than the other, or just different by chance.

blocks.title: The F‑Distribution

confusionCorner.body: The F‑distribution uses two degrees of freedom: one for the top variance, one for the bottom. [[imp:Don't mix them up.]] The numerator df comes from the sample with the larger variance.
confusionCorner.title: Two df Numbers, Not One!

explanation: The [[kw:F‑distribution]] is a curve used to compare two variances.
It is always skewed to the right. Values are zero or positive.
The shape depends on two numbers: [[imp:degrees of freedom for the top (numerator)]] and [[imp:degrees of freedom for the bottom (denominator)]].
We use an F‑table (Table 7) to find [[kw:critical values]]. Match the numerator df (column) and denominator df (row) for a given $\alpha$.

explanation: The [[kw:two‑sample F‑test]] compares two population variances.
Test statistic: $$F = \frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}$$ Always put the [[imp:larger sample variance in the numerator]] so F ≥ 1.
Degrees of freedom: numerator df = n₁ − 1, denominator df = n₂ − 1.
Hypotheses: $H_0$ usually says the variances are equal. $H_a$ can be one‑sided or two‑sided.
Three conditions: 1) random samples, 2) independent samples, 3) both populations normal.

confusionCorner.title: F‑Test Is Sensitive
confusionCorner.body: The F‑test assumes both populations are normal. If they are not normal, the test may give wrong results. [[imp:Always check the normality assumption.]]

blocks.title: The F‑Test Statistic

blocks.title: Example: Restaurant Wait Times

explanation: Old variance = 400, new variance = 256. Larger is old, so numerator: $F = 400/256 = 1.5625$.
Numerator df = 10 − 1 = 9, denominator df = 21 − 1 = 20.
We want to show old variance > new variance. So $H_0: \sigma_{old}^2 \le \sigma_{new}^2$, $H_a: \sigma_{old}^2 > \sigma_{new}^2$ (right‑tailed).
Critical value from α = 0.10 table with d.f.N=9, d.f.D=20 is 1.96.
$F = 1.56 < 1.96$, so fail to reject $H_0$. Not enough evidence the new system reduces variance.

discoveryHook.scenario: A manager wants to prove the new system has smaller variance in wait times. We'll test this at α = 0.10 using an F‑test.

confusionCorner.title: Small F, No Difference
confusionCorner.body: An F value close to 1 means the sample variances are similar. Even if one is a bit larger, it may not be statistically significant. [[imp:Only a large F (above critical value) shows a real difference.]]

What is the F‑statistic? (Answer to two decimals: 1.08)
With F = 1.08 < 2.11, we ___ to reject H₀.
hints: We do not have enough evidence.

explanation: **Understand**: Claim is A's variance < B's variance. B's variance is larger (2.8), so B is numerator. $H_0: \sigma_B^2 \le \sigma_A^2$, $H_a: \sigma_B^2 > \sigma_A^2$ (right‑tailed).
**Solve**: $F = 2.8/2.6 \approx 1.08$. Numerator df = 25−1=24, denominator df = 20−1=19. Critical value for α=0.05 is about 2.11.
**Conclude**: 1.08 < 2.11, fail to reject H₀. No evidence that A's variance is smaller.
